The Australian government’s controversial metadata retention scheme which allowed the government to store 2 years worth of personal data on citizen's online activities has been repealed after heated discussed in the senate, ending in a vote of 45-31.

The move comes in the wake of mass protests around the country which were sparked after the Australian government arrested a well known software pirate using evidence collected via metadata retention. In doing so, the government broke its promise to use collected metadata only in matters of national security, leaving many Australians feeling anxious about the reach of the government’s new found powers.

Opposition leader George Brandis has denounced the decision, accusing those who voted in favor of the schemes removal of being ‘soft on terrorism’. Prime Minister Ked Nelly, who voted in favor of the laws removal, responded to this accusation by politely reminding Mr. Brandis that there has been no evidence gathered from countries with similar laws to suggests that data retention aids in the prevention of terrorist attacks.

The Microstate Peace and Economic Summit has been productive so far. There has been an expansion of the invitee list due to widespread interest, and even larger nations such as Japan are sending their small or remote prefectures and provinces to connect with the rest of the world independently. A strong partnership will likely emerge from all this, but it won't be from all the meetings and closed-door conferences.

Last night, the St. Andrews police were called to the Old Course Hotel, where they found the bar in shambles and divots all over Hole #1 on the historic golf course.

The officer in charge, when asked for an update, said "When you see something like this...bottles of high-grade Scotch smashed on the floor, rare Scottish salmon caviar smeared on pictures of famous golfers...you imagine a group of powerful people, maybe even world leaders, getting drunk as hell and throwing caution to the wind and things out the windows."

"Well, that's exactly what happened."

Security cameras had apparently been disabled by hotel staff prior to the night's festivities, likely on a tip from the Scottish hosts, who had hinted to the possibility of mischief when they reserved the hotel into perpetuity and ordered several cases of Glenfidditch and Macallan to be put on hold for the week by local distilleries. There is little evidence of who is really to blame for the damage, other than dozens of presidents, crown princes, and prime ministers of various microstates the world over.

There is one piece of evidence, however, that was left at the scene. The flags of both Tuvalu and Liechtenstein were found planted together in Hole #1. Could this be a sign of diplomatic unity, or a prank requiring diplomatic immunity? We may never know, but additional evidence was found at the scene when Japan's delegate from the Ogasawara Islands was discovered passed out in the bathroom with a Fu Manchu drawn on him with permanent marker. This representative has been very popular at the summit, so this prank was likely done in jest. The representative was taken to the hotel infirmary for professional hydration.

The hotel was quiet when we arrived to do the story. Still, we couldn't help but think that the culprits were sitting in the shadows, watching us, waiting for us to leave so they could finish their round of midnight golf.
